semanticChecks.imperative: The original Ho Bala / U Vhala / Ku Hlaya constructions are infinitive or nominal title forms. The repaired Bala / Vhalani / Hlaya forms retain the source imperative. Same-module titles supply evidence that reading invisible forces is metaphorical in this course; with weather and landform objects and the slide body context, the construction is not about reading written text.
semanticChecks.windIdentity: Moya/Muya is supported by same-module references to damaging wind and wind direction. The word can also denote air (and in some usage spirit); the ordered weather/land-sign list and source body disambiguate it as wind here.
semanticChecks.objectOrder: Wind, Frost, Slope retained in source order.
semanticChecks.lessonNumber: Lesson 3 retained as Thuto 3 / Ngudo 3 / Dyondzo 3.
semanticChecks.slope: ST Letswapo is used in the same module for the land slope; VE u sendama ha mavu is explicitly paired with “slope” in same-module text and describes ground inclination, not soil slippage. TS keeps Slope in English.
semanticChecks.frost: Frost remains exactly in English in all three repaired candidates; ST Serame and VE Tshando are not substituted because they can refer to cold generally. TS xirhami is also a cold term and is not treated as an exact frost equivalent.

rows.specificEvidence: Same-module title uses “Ho Bala Matla a sa Bonweng” for reading invisible forces; course uses Moya for damaging wind/wind direction and letswapo for slope.
rows.remainingUncertainty: Imperative morphology and title idiom need fluent-speaker review; semantic recommendation is not fluency approval.

overallFinding: Repair all three proposed nominal Ho Bala / U Vhala / Ku Hlaya openings to imperative forms to match canonical Read. Preserve Frost in English; use existing same-module slope terms only where explicit source-paired context supports them. Current module language files are machine drafts, so no row is fluent-approved.
